section.title: Two Lines, Cain and Seth
section.sectionRationale: Two family lines are set side by side. Cain's line builds cities and culture and climbs to Lamech's boast of vengeance, while Seth's line ends with people calling on the name of the LORD. This closing section of chapter four traces where the two roads out of Eden are heading.
section.thesis: Away from God's presence one line builds a proud, violent civilization while another begins to call on the name of the LORD, and the whole Bible will follow these two roads to their ends.
section.frameNote: Two panels: the line of Cain from Enoch to Lamech's song of vengeance; and the line of Seth to Enosh, where worship of the LORD begins again.

verses.text: And Cain had relations with his wife, and she conceived and gave birth to Enoch. Then Cain built a {{city|city}} and named it after his son Enoch.
Now to Enoch was born Irad, and Irad was the father of Mehujael, and Mehujael was the father of Methusael, and Methusael was the father of Lamech.
And Lamech married two women, one named Adah and the other Zillah.
Adah gave birth to Jabal; he was the father of those who dwell in tents and raise livestock.
And his brother’s name was Jubal; he was the father of all who play the harp and flute.
And Zillah gave birth to Tubal-cain, a forger of every implement of bronze and iron. And the sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.
Then Lamech said to his wives: “Adah and Zillah, hear my voice; wives of Lamech, listen to my speech. For I have slain a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me.
If Cain is {{avenged|avenged}} sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold.”

units.label: The line of Seth
units.note: calling on the name of the LORD

verses.text: And Adam again had relations with his wife, and she gave birth to a son and named him Seth, saying, “God has granted me another {{seed|seed}} in place of Abel, since Cain killed him.”
And to Seth also a son was born, and he called him Enosh. At that time men began to {{call|call upon}} the name of the LORD.

city.gloss: A city or walled settlement. Cain, sentenced to be a restless wanderer, instead builds a city to secure himself and names it after his son. Human culture begins here, good gifts of art and craft mixed with a drive to build a home apart from God's presence.

avenged.gloss: To avenge, to take vengeance. God had promised sevenfold protection for Cain; Lamech seizes that language and boasts of seventy-sevenfold revenge for a mere wound. He turns a promise of restraint into a bragging charter for unlimited violence. Jesus overturns the number in Matthew 18:22.

seed.gloss: Offspring, seed. Eve confesses that God has granted another seed in place of murdered Abel. The promised line of 3:15 does not die with Abel; it continues through Seth, and Scripture will trace it down to Christ.

call.gloss: To call, to call out, to proclaim. In Seth's line people began to call on the name of the LORD, that is, to worship and pray to Him by name. Against Lamech's boast in his own name, a people rises who name and seek the LORD.

basic.context: The Bible now traces two families. Cain's descendants build cities, raise animals, make music, and forge tools, and they end with Lamech, a proud man who boasts about killing. Then we meet Seth's line, and the section ends with people beginning to worship God by name. The question is where each road is going.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real genealogy, but it is arranged to make a contrast. Cain's line shows culture racing ahead while violence deepens. Seth's line is quieter but turns toward God. The lesson is that progress in skill and comfort is not the same as being right with God.
basic.originalLanguages: Cain builds a city, an ir, to make himself safe. Lamech twists God's word about being avenged, naqam, into a boast of seventy-sevenfold revenge. But Eve calls Seth another seed, zera, in place of Abel, and in Seth's line people begin to call, qara, on the name of the LORD, to worship Him by name.
basic.typology: The seed given in place of Abel carries forward the promise of 3:15 that runs to Christ. And the two lines, one calling on the LORD and one boasting in itself, foreshadow the two humanities the whole Bible tracks, ending in the city of man and the city of God.
basic.christ: Lamech promises seventy-sevenfold vengeance; Jesus tells Peter to forgive seventy-seven times, undoing Lamech's boast with grace. And the seed granted in place of Abel keeps alive the line that leads to Jesus, the true seed who saves rather than avenges.
basic.god: God keeps His promise even after murder: the chosen line is not extinguished but continues through Seth. And God is the One whose name people begin to call upon, showing that He remains near to be worshipped even in a world drifting into violence.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 18 answers Lamech's seventy-sevenfold with forgiveness. Hebrews 11 lists the worshippers of faith who called on God. Jude warns against the way of Cain. Luke 3 traces Jesus' line back through Seth to Adam.
basic.oneStory: Two roads leave Eden. One builds a proud, self-secured, violent civilization; the other begins to call on the name of the LORD. The Bible will follow both to their ends, and the line of worship runs on toward Christ, while the line of boasting foreshadows the world He came to redeem.

context.literary:
Genesis 4:17-26 closes the movement that began at Genesis 2:4, 'the account of the heavens and the earth.' It sets two family lines side by side and lets the contrast speak without comment. The narrator does not say which line is good and which is not; he lets the endings do the work. Cain's line ends in a song of revenge, Seth's in prayer.

Cain's line is a straight genealogy of seven generations counting from Adam: Adam, Cain, Enoch, Irad, Mehujael, Methusael and Lamech. Lamech is therefore the seventh from Adam in this line. The detail matters, because in the line of Seth the seventh from Adam is Enoch, who 'walked with God,' Genesis 5:24, and Jude 1:14 calls him 'the seventh from Adam.' The seventh in one line boasts of killing; the seventh in the other walks with God and is taken by Him.

At Lamech the list opens out. He has two wives and four named children, three sons and a daughter, and each son is credited with a founding role: tent dwelling herdsmen, music, and metalwork. The genealogy of Seth in chapter 5 will also end with a father and three sons, Noah and Shem, Ham and Japheth, Genesis 5:32. Several names in the two lines look alike: Cain and Kenan, Irad and Jared, Mehujael and Mahalalel, Methusael and Methuselah, and both lines contain an Enoch and a Lamech. The similarity invites comparison of two men with nearly the same name and very different lives.

Lamech's words in verses 23 and 24 are the first poem in Cain's line and one of the earliest poems in the Bible. They are carefully built in parallel pairs: 'Adah and Zillah' and 'wives of Lamech,' 'hear my voice' and 'listen to my speech,' 'a man' and 'a young man,' 'sevenfold' and 'seventy-sevenfold.' The poetry is polished and the content is brutal. The first man's song in Genesis 2:23 praised his wife; this one threatens the world.

The section ends in verses 25 and 26 with a brief notice that restarts the line of promise. It prepares directly for the genealogy of Genesis 5, which begins, 'This is the book of the generations of Adam,' Genesis 5:1, and traces the line of Seth to Noah.
context.historical:
The passage describes the rise of settled civilization in a few lines: a city, herding in tents, music and metalwork. These were the achievements that marked the great cultures of the ancient Near East. Mesopotamian traditions credited the gods or semi-divine sages with giving humanity the arts of civilization, kingship, the city, crafts and music. Genesis tells it differently. These things came from human beings, specifically from the descendants of Cain, and they are presented as human achievements, not divine revelations.

For Israel this was an important correction. The cities, instruments and weapons of the nations around them were impressive, and the Israelites often felt small by comparison. In the days of Saul there was no blacksmith in Israel, and the Israelites had to go down to the Philistines to sharpen their tools, 1 Samuel 13:19-20. Genesis tells them that such skills are neither divine nor a measure of righteousness. The line that first mastered them also produced Lamech.

The mention of 'bronze and iron' in verse 22 describes the working of metals that would later shape warfare and agriculture alike. The harp and flute of verse 21 were the instruments of both worship and revelry. David played the harp before Saul, 1 Samuel 16:23, and Israel praised God 'with strings and flute,' Psalm 150:4. The wicked of Job 21:12 make merry to the same instruments.

Lamech's marriage to two wives is the first mention of polygamy in the Bible. Israel lived among peoples where it was common among the powerful, and Genesis will later show its bitter fruit in the rivalry of Rachel and Leah, Genesis 30:1, and of Hannah and her rival, 1 Samuel 1:6. The law warned kings not to 'take many wives,' Deuteronomy 17:17. Set against Genesis 2:24, Lamech's household is already a departure from the design.

Lamech's boast reflects the ancient practice of blood vengeance, in which a family avenged a killing. Israel's law restrained that practice with cities of refuge and a command: 'Do not seek revenge,' Leviticus 19:18.
context.canonical:
The two lines of Genesis 4 are the first sketch of a division that runs through the whole Bible. The line of Seth continues in Genesis 5 through Enoch and Noah, and later through Shem to Abraham. The line of Cain vanishes from the record after this chapter, but its spirit reappears. At Babel people build a city and a tower 'that we may make a name for ourselves,' Genesis 11:4, and God scatters them. Immediately afterward God promises Abram, 'I will make your name great,' Genesis 12:2. The name that humanity grasps for is given by God to the one who trusts Him. Psalm 49:11 speaks of the wealthy whose graves are their eternal homes 'even though their lands were their namesakes,' echoing Cain's city named after his son.

The phrase 'call upon the name of the LORD' becomes a thread through Scripture. Abram builds an altar and calls on the name of the LORD, Genesis 12:8 and 13:4, as does Isaac, Genesis 26:25. The psalmist in distress calls on the name of the LORD, Psalm 116:4, and promises to do so with thanksgiving, Psalm 116:17. Joel 2:32 promises that 'everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved,' and Zephaniah 3:9 foresees the peoples calling on His name together.

The New Testament takes up both lines. Peter quotes Joel at Pentecost, Acts 2:21, and Paul applies it to Jesus, Romans 10:13, and describes Christians as 'all those everywhere who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,' 1 Corinthians 1:2. Luke's genealogy of Jesus runs through 'the son of Enosh, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God,' Luke 3:38. Jesus answers Lamech's seventy-sevenfold with seventy-seven times of forgiveness, Matthew 18:22. And Revelation 18:22 announces that in fallen Babylon the sound of harpists, flute players and craftsmen will never be heard again, while the holy city comes down from God, Revelation 21:2.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to see where the two paths out of Eden lead. On one path humanity builds, invents and grows powerful, but moves further from God and deeper into violence. On the other path humanity is weak, mortal and quiet, but calls on the name of the LORD. The contrast teaches that the measure of a people is not their achievements but their relationship to God.

He also wanted Israel to value culture rightly. The skills of Cain's descendants are real gifts. Herding, music and metalwork are good, and Israel would use all of them in its life and worship. But Moses shows that these gifts can be developed by people who have no fear of God and used for pride and violence. Culture is not salvation.

He wanted them to hear the danger of revenge. Lamech takes God's word of protection over Cain and turns it into a weapon, inflating it into a claim to unlimited vengeance. Israel would receive a law that limited retaliation and forbade personal revenge, and Moses shows here what humanity becomes without such restraint.

Finally, he wanted them to take hope in God's faithfulness. After the murder of Abel and the exile of Cain it might seem that the promise of Genesis 3:15 had failed. But God gives Seth, 'another seed in place of Abel,' and in Seth's line people begin to call on the LORD. The promised line survives, and so does worship.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The genealogies describe history; they do not command anyone to build cities, raise livestock, play instruments or forge tools, nor do they forbid it. Cain's city and Lamech's inventions are recorded, not endorsed or condemned in themselves.

Some features are clearly presented as negative examples. Lamech's two wives depart from the pattern of Genesis 2:24, and Jesus later calls marriage back to how it was 'from the beginning,' Matthew 19:8. Lamech's song glorifies violence and revenge, and Scripture elsewhere is plain: 'Do not seek revenge,' Leviticus 19:18, and 'Do not avenge yourselves,' Romans 12:19. His example is recorded as a warning.

The note in verse 26 about calling on the name of the LORD is descriptive, but it describes something Scripture everywhere commends. Calling on the LORD in prayer, worship and trust is the right response of mortal people to their God, and in the New Testament it becomes the mark of those who belong to Christ, 1 Corinthians 1:2. What carries forward is not a particular form of culture but the call to worship God and to reject the pride and vengeance of Lamech.

debates.question: Is Cain's line condemned for its culture, or only for its pride and violence?

views.label: The whole project is a bid for life without God
views.case: Cain was sentenced to be a wanderer, yet he builds a city, verse 17, and names it after his son rather than calling on God. The line that follows advances in skill but climaxes in Lamech's violence. On this reading the city and its culture are the first attempt to build security and a name apart from God, anticipating Babel, Genesis 11:4.

views.label: Culture is a good gift misused
views.case: Herding, music and metalwork reflect the creative image of God and the mandate to fill and subdue the earth, Genesis 1:28. Later Scripture honours craft, as when God fills Bezalel with His Spirit for artistic work, Exodus 31:3, and uses music in worship. The condemnation falls on Lamech's pride and violence, not on the skills themselves.

debates.bearing: The text holds both truths. The gifts are good, and God's people will use them. But in Cain's line they develop apart from God, and the passage warns that progress in skill can go hand in hand with moral decline.

debates.question: Where did Cain's wife come from?

views.label: A sister or other close relative
views.case: Genesis 5:4 says Adam had 'other sons and daughters,' and Acts 17:26 says God made every nation 'from one man.' On this view Cain married a sister or niece. Marriage between close relatives was later forbidden, Leviticus 18:9, but that law came much later, when the human family had grown.

views.label: The text does not tell us
views.case: Genesis is not writing a complete family history. It mentions only the people who matter for its argument. Cain's fear that 'whoever finds me will kill me,' Genesis 4:14, already assumes other people, and the narrator does not stop to explain who they are.

debates.bearing: The simplest answer consistent with Scripture is that Cain married a close relative from Adam's wider family. The text's silence is a reminder that Genesis is selective, focused on the line of promise rather than on answering every question a modern reader brings.

debates.question: What began in the days of Enosh?

views.label: Public or regular worship of the LORD
views.case: Most read verse 26 as the start of formal prayer and worship using God's covenant name, perhaps communal and public, the same practice Abram continues when he builds altars and calls on the name of the LORD, Genesis 12:8. It sits against Exodus 6:3, where God says He did not make Himself known to the patriarchs by the name the LORD, which is usually understood to mean that they knew the name but not the full revelation of its meaning in the exodus.

views.label: Prayer arising from human frailty
views.case: Enosh means 'man' in the sense of mortal humanity, Psalm 8:4. Some read the naming and the calling together: as people recognised their weakness, they turned to the LORD for help.

views.label: The beginning of false worship
views.case: The BSB footnote notes that some translate the verb as 'to profane.' Some medieval Jewish commentators, Rashi among them, read the verse as the beginning of idolatry, when people began to give the divine name to created things.

debates.bearing: The context strongly favours a positive reading. The verse stands in deliberate contrast to Lamech's boast and leads directly into the godly line of chapter 5. It marks the survival of true worship in a violent world.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb in verse 17 describing Cain's building is a participle with the verb 'to be,' literally 'he was building a city.' It suggests an ongoing project rather than a single act, as though Cain spent his restless life building something permanent. The name he gives the city, Enoch, is chanok, related to the verb chanak, to dedicate. The same verb is used of dedicating a new house, Deuteronomy 20:5, and of dedicating the temple, 1 Kings 8:63. Cain dedicates a city to his son's name; the psalmist later speaks of those whose 'lands were their namesakes,' Psalm 49:11.

Jubal is the 'father of all who play the harp and flute,' verse 21. The harp is kinnor, a stringed instrument like a lyre, the instrument David played before Saul, 1 Samuel 16:23. The flute is ugab, the instrument named in Job 21:12 and in the last psalm, 'Praise Him with strings and flute,' Psalm 150:4. The word 'father' here means founder or originator, the first of a guild, not a literal father of every musician.

Tubal-cain is 'a forger of every implement of bronze and iron,' verse 22. The word 'forger' comes from a verb meaning to sharpen, used of God who 'will sharpen His sword,' Psalm 7:12. The metals are nechoshet, bronze or copper, and barzel, iron. The same skills that make ploughs make swords, a tension Isaiah 2:4 resolves when he foresees swords beaten into plowshares.

Lamech's poem in verses 23 and 24 uses the formal language of a public address: 'hear my voice,' and 'listen to my speech.' Isaiah uses a similar paired summons, 'Listen and hear my voice,' Isaiah 28:23. 'Young man' is yeled, a word usually meaning child or boy, which some read as a sign of the pettiness and disproportion of his vengeance. The numbers escalate from God's sevenfold protection of Cain, verse 15, to Lamech's seventy-sevenfold. The BSB footnote notes that the Greek of verse 24 can be read either as seventy times seven or seventy-sevenfold, and points to Matthew 18:22. Jesus' answer to Peter uses the same Greek expression as the Septuagint of this verse, turning Lamech's measure of revenge into the measure of forgiveness.

Seth's name in verse 25 plays on the verb shit, to set or appoint. The BSB footnote explains that Seth 'probably means granted or appointed,' and Eve's words, 'God has granted me,' use that verb. Seth is appointed in place of Abel.

Enosh in verse 26 is a common noun for 'man,' usually with a sense of human frailty. It is the word in 'what is man that You are mindful of him,' Psalm 8:4, and 'As for man, his days are like grass,' Psalm 103:15. Adam means humanity drawn from the ground; Enosh means humanity in its weakness. The verse that names him then describes people beginning to call on the LORD.

The phrase 'call upon the name of the LORD' uses qara with the preposition 'in' or 'on' and the name. It can mean to invoke, to pray, or to proclaim, and the BSB footnote lists 'to proclaim,' 'to invoke,' and 'to call themselves by' as possibilities. The verb 'began' is from a root that can also mean to profane, which is why the same footnote mentions that reading. The same expression describes Abraham's worship at his altars, Genesis 12:8 and 21:33.

typology.type: Seth, the seed appointed in place of Abel, Genesis 4:25
typology.fulfillment: Eve calls Seth 'another seed,' recalling the seed of the woman promised in Genesis 3:15. The promise that seemed threatened by Abel's death continues through a son appointed by God. Luke's genealogy traces Jesus back through 'the son of Enosh, the son of Seth, the son of Adam,' Luke 3:38. Paul speaks of God sending His Son 'born of a woman,' Galatians 4:4. The pattern escalates: Seth replaced the murdered righteous man, but Christ is the murdered righteous man who rises again, so that He needs no replacement. Seth carried the line forward; Christ is the one to whom the line was always heading.

typology.type: The two lines, the city builders and those who call on the LORD
typology.fulfillment: The division between Cain's line and Seth's becomes a lasting pattern. Cain builds a city and names it after his son; later Babel builds a city to make a name, Genesis 11:4, and Babylon becomes the great city of human pride, Daniel 4:30. Abraham, by contrast, looks 'forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God,' Hebrews 11:10. Revelation shows Babylon falling, its music and craft silenced, Revelation 18:22, and the holy city coming down from God, Revelation 21:2. The type falls short because the lines of Genesis are genealogical; in Christ the two humanities are defined by faith, not ancestry.

typology.type: Calling on the name of the LORD, Genesis 4:26
typology.fulfillment: In the days of Enosh people began to call on the name of the LORD, and the phrase becomes a summary of true worship through the Old Testament, as with Abraham at his altars. Joel promises that 'everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved,' Joel 2:32. Paul quotes it and applies the name to Jesus, 'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved,' Romans 10:13, and describes Christians as those 'who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,' 1 Corinthians 1:2. What began as a small movement in one family becomes the worship of every tribe and tongue, Revelation 5:9.

This is a type by contrast. Lamech takes God's promise of sevenfold protection and multiplies it into seventy-sevenfold revenge. Jesus reverses it: when Peter asks whether he should forgive seven times, Jesus answers, 'not just seven times, but seventy-seven times,' Matthew 18:22, using the same expression the Greek Old Testament uses here. Christ does not merely teach this; when He suffered 'He did not retaliate,' 1 Peter 2:23, and prayed for His enemies. Lamech's song is answered by the cross, where unlimited vengeance gives way to unlimited mercy.

study.christ:
This passage leads to Christ first by promise. After Abel's murder and Cain's exile, it might have seemed that the seed promised in Genesis 3:15 had been lost. But Eve names Seth 'another seed in place of Abel,' Genesis 4:25. The word seed deliberately recalls the promise. The line of promise continues through Seth, and Luke traces Jesus' ancestry through 'the son of Enosh, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God,' Luke 3:38. The quiet line of Seth is the road on which the Messiah would come.

It leads to Christ by contrast with Lamech. Lamech is the opposite of the Saviour. He boasts of killing a young man for wounding him, and he inflates God's protection of Cain into a claim to unlimited vengeance. Jesus answers him directly. When Peter asks how many times he should forgive, Jesus says, 'not just seven times, but seventy-seven times,' Matthew 18:22, the same measure Lamech used for revenge. Jesus taught His followers not to retaliate against evil, Matthew 5:39, and He lived what He taught. 'When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate,' 1 Peter 2:23. Lamech was wounded and killed; Christ was wounded and died for those who wounded Him.

It leads to Christ through worship. The chapter ends with people beginning to call on the name of the LORD. The New Testament applies that very phrase to Jesus. Peter at Pentecost quotes Joel, 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved,' Acts 2:21, and then calls his hearers to be baptized 'in the name of Jesus Christ,' Acts 2:38. Paul says the same Lord is Lord of all and 'gives richly to all who call on Him,' Romans 10:12-13. Calling on the name of the LORD, begun in the days of Enosh, becomes calling on the name of Jesus.

It leads to Christ through the city. Cain builds a city for his son; the builders of Babel try to make a name for themselves. Christ does not build an earthly city but prepares a heavenly one. Abraham looked for 'the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God,' Hebrews 11:10, and Hebrews says God 'has prepared a city' for His people, Hebrews 11:16. In Revelation the new Jerusalem comes down from God, and into it the nations bring their glory, Revelation 21:24-26. The skills that began in Cain's line, music and craft, will find their true purpose in the worship of the Lamb.

A caution is needed. The passage does not present Seth as a type of Christ in any explicit way, and the details of Cain's city or Lamech's sons are not coded pictures of the gospel. The links drawn here rest on the promise of the seed, on Jesus' own answer to Lamech, and on the New Testament's use of the language of calling on the name of the Lord.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who keeps His promises even when human history seems to be going the other way. Cain's line grows in power and skill, and its most famous member boasts of murder. The righteous Abel is dead. Yet God grants Eve another son, and through Seth the line of promise continues. God's purposes are not defeated by human violence.

He is the God who gives. Eve's words at Seth's birth are 'God has granted me another seed,' verse 25. She sees the child as God's gift and as His answer to loss. At Cain's birth she said she had brought forth a man with the LORD's help; now she says God has appointed a son. The emphasis has moved from what she has done to what God has given.

He is the God whose name can be called upon. The chapter closes with people beginning to call on the name of the LORD, verse 26. God is not a distant force or an unknown power; He has a name, He can be addressed, and He answers. His covenant name is already on the lips of His people in the earliest generations.

He is also the God who reserves vengeance to Himself. God had said that anyone who killed Cain would be avenged sevenfold, verse 15, a word of protection meant to restrain violence. Lamech takes that word and twists it to justify his own revenge. Scripture consistently says that vengeance belongs to God alone, 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,' Deuteronomy 32:35, and He exercises it with justice, not with the disproportion of Lamech. Psalm 94:1 calls on Him as 'God of vengeance' precisely because human vengeance cannot be trusted.

He is the source of the gifts even of those who do not honour Him. The skills of Jabal, Jubal and Tubal-cain are real, and they come from human beings made in God's image. God does not withdraw His common kindness from Cain's line; He lets them build, make music and forge tools. The same God later fills Bezalel with His Spirit for craftsmanship, Exodus 31:3, and receives the praise of harp and flute, Psalm 150:3-4.

The passage holds a tension. God allows the line of Cain to flourish in culture while it declines in righteousness, and He allows the line of Seth to be small and quiet. Human greatness and divine favour do not always coincide. God's faithfulness is often seen not in the loud achievements of the powerful but in the quiet prayers of the weak.

For worship, the passage calls us to call on the name of the LORD, to receive our children and our gifts as from His hand, to leave vengeance to Him, and to use every skill we have for His glory rather than for our own name.

crossReferences.note: Peter asks whether he should forgive his brother up to seven times, and Jesus answers, 'not just seven times, but seventy-seven times.' The number deliberately answers Lamech's seventy-sevenfold vengeance of Genesis 4:24, turning a measure of revenge into a measure of mercy.

Luke traces Jesus' genealogy back through Lamech, Methuselah, Enoch, Jared, Mahalalel, Cainan and Enosh to Seth and Adam, 'the son of God.' The line that began with the seed granted in place of Abel leads to Christ.

Paul says the same Lord is Lord of all and gives richly to all who call on Him, for 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.' The practice that began in the days of Enosh becomes the way of salvation for Jew and Gentile alike.

The builders of Babel say, 'let us build for ourselves a city with a tower,' so 'that we may make a name for ourselves.' They follow the pattern of Cain, who built a city and named it after his son, seeking security and a name apart from God.
Abram builds an altar and calls on the name of the LORD. The worship that began in the days of Enosh, Genesis 4:26, continues in the man God has chosen to carry the promise forward.

Jude calls Enoch 'the seventh from Adam.' In Seth's line the seventh generation is Enoch, who walked with God; in Cain's line the seventh is Lamech, who boasts of murder. The two sevenths show where the two roads lead.
Abraham was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God. Cain built a city for his own name; the people of faith wait for the city God Himself builds.

In the fall of Babylon the sound of harpists and flute players will never be heard again, and no craftsman will be found in her. The music and craft that began in Cain's line, when used by the proud city of man, come to an end under God's judgment.

Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved. Joel takes the phrase of Genesis 4:26 and makes it the promise of salvation in the day of the LORD, a promise Peter declares fulfilled at Pentecost, Acts 2:21.

Paul tells believers not to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's wrath, quoting 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay.' It is the direct answer to Lamech, who claimed a vengeance that belongs to God alone.

God fills Bezalel with His Spirit and with skill in every kind of craftsmanship for the building of the tabernacle. The arts that began in Cain's line are not evil in themselves; God gives them to His people for His worship.

'What is man that You are mindful of him?' The word for man here is enosh, the name of Seth's son. The psalm expresses the wonder that God should care for frail humanity, the same humanity that in Enosh's day began to call on His name.

study.oneStory:
This passage completes the account that began in Genesis 2:4. It shows the world after Eden dividing into two paths. One path is the line of Cain: impressive, inventive and increasingly violent, the beginnings of the city of man. The other is the line of Seth: small, mortal and quiet, but calling on the name of the LORD. The question the passage answers is what happens to humanity after the fall. It flourishes in skill and falls in righteousness, and yet God keeps a people for Himself.

It sets up what follows immediately. Genesis 5 traces Seth's line through Enoch, who walked with God, to Noah, whose father hoped he would bring comfort from the cursed ground, Genesis 5:29. By Genesis 6 violence fills the earth, and the flood comes. Only Noah, from Seth's line, 'found favor in the eyes of the LORD,' Genesis 6:8. The pattern of two lines continues after the flood, in Babel's city and in the call of Abraham, who calls on the name of the LORD and looks for a city God builds.

The rest of the Old Testament keeps both paths in view. Israel is called to be the people who call on the name of the LORD, and yet it is repeatedly tempted by the power and culture of the nations. The prophets warn against trusting in cities, weapons and wealth, and they promise a day when swords will be beaten into plowshares, Isaiah 2:4, and when all the peoples will call on the name of the LORD, Zephaniah 3:9.

In Christ the two lines meet their end and their answer. He comes from the line of Seth, the promised seed. He overturns Lamech's vengeance with forgiveness and bears the violence of the world on the cross. And He makes calling on His name the way of salvation for everyone, from every nation.

In the new creation the city of man falls and the city of God comes down from heaven. Babylon's music is silenced, Revelation 18:22, but in the new Jerusalem the nations bring their glory and honour, Revelation 21:24-26. The skills first developed in Cain's line are redeemed and used in worship, and the whole people of God, a multitude from every tribe and tongue, call on the name of the Lord forever.

quiz.q: What is the main contrast between the line of Cain and the line of Seth?

options.text: Cain's line boasts in itself and its violence, while Seth's line begins to call on the name of the LORD.
options.note: The two lines picture two roads, self-exaltation and worship.

options.text: Cain's line was poor while Seth's line was wealthy.
options.note: The contrast is spiritual, not about wealth; Cain's line is actually rich in culture.

options.text: Cain's line had no children while Seth's line multiplied.
options.note: Both lines have descendants; the difference is their direction toward or away from God.

options.text: There is no real contrast; both lines are the same.
options.note: The passage is built to set the two lines against each other.

quiz.q: What does Lamech's song reveal about the line of Cain?

options.text: It has grown proud and boasts openly in vengeance and violence.
options.note: Lamech turns God's promise of protection into a charter for revenge.

options.text: It has become sorrowful and repentant over sin.
options.note: The opposite; Lamech boasts rather than repents.

options.text: It has simply grown skilled in music and metalwork.
options.note: The skills are real, but the song exposes the deeper problem of pride and violence.

options.text: It has turned back to worship the LORD.
options.note: That describes Seth's line, not Lamech.

quiz.q: Why does Eve call Seth another seed in place of Abel?

options.text: The promised line of the woman's seed continues through Seth after Abel's death.
options.note: God preserves the chosen line that leads toward Christ.

options.text: Seth was simply her favorite child.
options.note: There is hope in her words, but the point is God's faithfulness to the promise, not favoritism.

options.text: Seth would avenge Abel's murder on Cain.
options.note: Nothing here speaks of vengeance; Seth carries the line of promise.

options.text: It means nothing beyond naming a baby.
options.note: Eve's words point to God granting a seed to continue the promise.

quiz.q: How does Jesus respond to Lamech's cry of seventy-sevenfold vengeance?

options.text: He calls His people to forgive seventy-seven times, replacing vengeance with mercy.
options.note: Matthew 18:22 deliberately overturns Lamech's boast.

options.text: He commands even greater vengeance on enemies.
options.note: The reverse; Jesus overturns vengeance with forgiveness.

options.text: He says vengeance should be limited to seven times only.
options.note: Jesus does not cap revenge; He replaces it with abundant forgiveness.

options.text: He never addresses anything like Lamech's boast.
options.note: His seventy-seven times clearly answers Lamech's seventy-sevenfold.

quiz.q: What began in the line of Seth at the time of Enosh?

options.text: People began to call on the name of the LORD, that is, to worship Him by name.
options.note: Public worship of the LORD rises in Seth's line.

options.text: People began to build the first cities.
options.note: That was Cain's line; Seth's line is marked by worship.

options.text: People began to forge tools of bronze and iron.
options.note: That is Tubal-cain in Cain's line, not Seth's.

options.text: People stopped believing in God altogether.
options.note: The opposite; they began to call on the LORD.

questions: Cain's line was gifted with real skill in music, craft, and building, yet drifted from God. Where might your own talents and progress be quietly pulling you away from Him instead of toward Him?
Lamech boasted about getting his own back and multiplying revenge. Where are you keeping score against someone, and what would it look like to hand that to God instead?
The line of Seth is remembered for beginning to call on the name of the LORD. What does calling on God look like in the ordinary rhythm of your week?
God preserved the promised line even after murder and heartbreak. Where do you need to trust that God is still keeping His promises when your own story feels broken?
Two roads run through this passage, one building a name for itself and one seeking God's name. Which road are your daily choices actually laying down for those who come after you?

translationNotes.note: Began to call upon the name of the LORD can also be rendered began to proclaim the name of the LORD, or, in some traditions, to call themselves by the name of the LORD; each reading points to the beginning of public worship in Seth's line.
